implementation_notes: The component-tree realization: an ancestor wraps its child content in a cascading value (or registers it at the root with builder.Services.AddCascadingValue) and any descendant declares [CascadingParameter] to receive it - optionally under a Name - so the components in between never see the value. CascadingValueSource<T> with isFixed: false adds update notifications (set isFixed: true when the value cannot change, because subscriptions cost). Remember that cascading values are not services: the docs warn that registering a component type as a cascading value does not register services or permit service activation for it.
code_sketch:
<CascadingValue Value="theme">
    <Layout />
</CascadingValue>

@code {
    [CascadingParameter] private Theme? Theme { get; set; }
}
pitfalls: Cascading values are matched by type unless you give them a Name - two cascading values of the same type silently collide and the consumer gets the nearest one.
With isFixed: false every subscriber is notified on any state change of the class, and the docs recommend granular classes because a change to one property re-renders all subscribers.
A subtree rendered with static server-side rendering cannot receive update notifications, so a cascading value that must change needs an interactive render mode.

variants.name: AsyncLocal<T> ambient data for an asynchronous flow
variants.implementation_notes: On the server there is no component tree, so the ambient carrier is AsyncLocal<T>: a value written inside a flow is visible to everything the flow calls, including continuations after an await, because the ExecutionContext is copied rather than tied to a thread (contrast ThreadLocal<T>, which is thread-affine and therefore wrong as soon as code awaits). It has no nearest-provider semantics: nested scopes must save and restore the previous value by hand, and nothing clears it for you when the request ends.
pitfalls: A write inside an awaited call does not flow back to the caller - the async context is copied, so the caller keeps its own value.
A value left set is visible to whatever runs next on that flow; with pooling and long-lived contexts this leaks request state across requests.
Nesting must restore, not null: save the previous value and put it back in a finally block, or the outer scope ends up with the inner value.
